title: Luminosity, Size and Temperature
short: A star's power is L = 4πR²σT⁴, so in solar units L = R²T⁴.
trouble: Students think a hotter star must always be more luminous, forgetting that size matters too.

blocks.html: A star's luminosity $L$ is its total power: the energy it sends out each second, in watts. The Sun's is $3.83 \times 10^{26}$ W. From Wien's law you know temperature sets a star's color. Temperature also sets how much power each square meter of its surface gives off, and the size of the surface does the rest.

Each square meter of a hot surface radiates $\sigma T^4$ watts (the Stefan–Boltzmann law, with $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{W/(m}^2\text{K}^4)$). The fourth power is steep: double the temperature and each square meter gives off $2^4 = 16$ times as much. A star's surface is a sphere of area $4\pi R^2$. So $$L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4.$$ Divide by the Sun's values and every constant cancels: in solar units (radius in $R_\odot$, temperature in units of the Sun's $5772$ K), $L = R^2 T^4$. The exponent rules make this quick: $(2R)^2 = 4R^2$ and $(2T)^4 = 16T^4$.

$L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$; in solar units, $L = R^2 T^4$. Luminosity depends on size and temperature together, so a cool star can be very luminous if it is huge, and a hot star can be faint if it is tiny.

blocks.cap: Luminosity against temperature (hotter to the left). The dashed lines are stars of equal radius: from $0.01$ to $1000$ solar radii.

blocks.title: A giant star
blocks.q: A star is $10$ times the Sun's radius and has half the Sun's surface temperature. Find its luminosity.
steps: $L = 6.25$ solar luminosities: cooler, yet more luminous, because it is so big.

blocks.title: A white dwarf
blocks.q: A star is $0.01$ times as luminous as the Sun but twice as hot. What is its radius?
steps: That is about $17{,}000$ km, less than three times Earth's radius: a white dwarf.

blocks.title: Check with the Sun
blocks.q: Use $R = 6.96 \times 10^{8}$ m and $T = 5772$ K to find the Sun's luminosity.

blocks.html: It seems that a hotter star should always be more luminous, but size matters as much. Sirius B is about $25{,}000$ K, over four times hotter than the Sun, yet it gives off only a few percent of the Sun's power, because it is about the size of Earth. Check with $L = R^2 T^4$: a tiny $R$ can outweigh a big $T$.

blocks.name: ph-blackbody
blocks.cap: The area under each curve is the power per square meter, $\sigma T^4$. A $7000$ K surface gives off $(7000/5772)^4 \approx 2.2$ times as much as the Sun's.
